rule: good. the gerund subject is read as an occurrence trigger rather than a thing, so this parses as a fireable rule: every sky-cat hunting event yields a reduction of nightmoth populations, with the two linked.
texts: good. parses as a fireable rule keyed on the descending event, with the same cats carried into the hunting and the response tied to its trigger.

mixed: the rule fires and records that hunting shrinks a nightmoth crowd, but 'that lantern-row' has no antecedent anywhere in the sentence, so the translator invents a specific crowd and a specific row and shrinks that one crowd no matter where the hunting happened — the link between where the cats hunt and which crowd shrinks is lost. Introduce the row in the trigger clause: 'When sky-cats hunt nightmoths at a lantern-row, the nightmoth crowd at that lantern-row shrinks.'

bad: the trigger came out as a standing kind-level fact about sky-cats and nightmoths, which no actual hunting event ever produces, so this rule can never fire on evidence; 'that lantern-row' is left dangling as in the previous sentence, and the thinning is one shared event rather than one per occasion. Name the row in the trigger and use the explicit occurrence wording: 'Whenever sky-cats hunt nightmoths at a lantern-row, the nightmoth crowd at that lantern-row thins.'

mixed: the 'after' ordering and the falling harvest are recorded correctly, but the trigger is the compound kind 'sky-cat hunt', which only a sentence literally using that noun phrase would produce — a normal sentence about sky-cats hunting will not set it off — and 'that lantern-row' again has no antecedent, so the harvest is a free-standing specific thing unconnected to the hunt.
